newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan jobless rate edges down but problems linger.
newsitem.headline: Japan jobless rate edges down but problems linger.

text.p: Japan's jobless rate edged down in August, continuing a steady drop from record highs, but the worst may not be over yet, particularly for older workers.
The government announced Tuesday that the unemployment rate fell to 3.3 percent in August after dropping to 3.4 percent in July from a record high of 3.5 percent in the preceding two months.

But the good news was tempered by some discouraging data, such as a slight drop in job openings and a rise in unemployment among older age groups -- signs of sluggish economic recovery and a continuing process of painful corporate restructuring.

"Unemployment has dropped for the second month in a row. But there are still worrying factors such as an increase in middle-aged and older unemployed people," an official at the government's Management and Coordination Agency said.

Although Japan does not have the double-digit jobless rates of some Western countries, a climb in the rate over the past year has rattled a nation that has had minimal unemployment for most of the postwar era.

The jobless rate among workers aged over 55 rose by 0.9 percentage point to 4.2 percent in August as Japanese companies continued to streamline their operations and cut wage costs in the face of a prolonged business slump.
The agency official said the main reasons for the drop in the overall figure was a modest decline in the number of young unemployed and an increase in female part-time workers.
"We cannot say definitely that there has been a change in the basic jobless trend," the official said.
A fall in job openings, a closely watched barometer of the employment situation, was one cause for concern.
Job openings, which had risen for the third month in a row in July, fell to 71 for every 100 job seekers in August from 72 openings in July.
"The drop in the job openings may be a sign of a sluggish economic recovery," Satoshi Shimamoto, a senior economist at MMS International, told Reuters Financial Television.
He said there will be increased pressure on Japanese firms to reduce the number of mature workers on their payrolls as these tend to be the highly paid portion of the work force.
Analysts said the jobless rate could rise again if the tentative recovery in the economy slows down or comes to a halt.

Despite government stimulus steps, the economy has been struggling to recover from a slump that set in after the bursting of the economic "bubble" of the late 1980s, forcing companies to cut costs and restructure their operations to maintain profits. Many analysts predict the recovery will slow in early 1997, especially after a planned rise in the sales tax to 5 percent from 3 percent from next April.
